proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(\beta_R=v\) and \(\beta_A=h\).  For the selected prefixes and terminal suffixes define
\[
 R=\begin{bmatrix}\alpha M_{u_1}\\ \vdots\\ \alpha M_{u_K}\end{bmatrix},
 \qquad
 C=\begin{bmatrix}M_{w_1}\beta_{b_1}&\cdots&M_{w_K}\beta_{b_K}\end{bmatrix}.
\]
By the stopped-series definition, for every \(i,j\) and \(a\in\mathcal Y\),
\[
 H[i,j]=\alpha M_{u_i}M_{w_j}\beta_{b_j},
 \qquad
 H_a[i,j]=\alpha M_{u_i}M_aM_{w_j}\beta_{b_j}.
\]
Consequently
\[
 H=RC,
 \qquad
 H_a=RM_aC.                                                    \tag{1}
\]
The hidden Markov construction is a \(K\)-dimensional linear realization, so every stopped Hankel submatrix has rank at most \(K\).  Conversely, any \(d\)-dimensional linear realization factors every Hankel submatrix as a prefix matrix with \(d\) columns times a suffix matrix with \(d\) rows and therefore has Hankel rank at most \(d\).  The assumed rank \(K\) of the full finite two-terminal array thus implies that no realization of dimension less than \(K\) exists.  The given realization is therefore minimal, and rank \(K\) also implies that at least one \(K\)-by-\(K\) minor is nonsingular.  This rank assertion alone says nothing about which minor is nonsingular, so it does not imply \(\det H_{\mathcal U,\mathcal V}\ne0\) for a tuple fixed in advance.

Now suppose the declared minor is valid.  Since \(R\) and \(C\) in (1) are square and \(RC=H\) is invertible, both \(R\) and \(C\) are invertible.  Hence
\[
 H^{-1}H_a=C^{-1}M_aC.                                         \tag{2}
\]
Because \(u_1=\epsilon\), the first row of \(H=RC\) is \(\alpha C\); this is precisely the empty-prefix coordinate row, and therefore
\[
 \bar\alpha=\alpha C.                                         \tag{3}
\]
For the terminal columns \(f_R=(F_R(u_i))_{i=1}^K=Rv\) and \(f_A=(F_A(u_i))_{i=1}^K=Rh\), equation (1) gives
\[
 H^{-1}f_R=C^{-1}v,
 \qquad
 H^{-1}f_A=C^{-1}h.                                            \tag{4}
\]
Equations (2)--(4) are exactly the displayed canonical formulas:
\[
 \bar M_a=C^{-1}M_aC,
 \qquad
 \bar\alpha=\alpha C,
 \qquad
 \bar v=C^{-1}v,
 \qquad
 \bar h=C^{-1}h.                                               \tag{5}
\]

If a second minimal \(K\)-dimensional realization generates the same stopped series, applying the same observable minor to it again produces the unique matrices and vectors on the left side of (5).  If its suffix matrix is \(\widetilde C\), then both original realizations are related to this common canonical realization, and hence to each other, by the single invertible similarity \(C\widetilde C^{-1}\) (with the corresponding inverse convention for columns).  Thus one common similarity transports every letter operator and both terminal columns.

Finally, each entry of \(H\) uses a word of length at most \(2K-2\), while each entry of \(H_a\) uses a word of length at most \((K-1)+1+(K-1)=2K-1\).  The terminal columns use no longer words.  The horizon assumption \(T\ge2K-1\) therefore makes every quantity in (5) a coordinate of the observed stopped law.  This proves all three assertions.

Work first in a legal latent coordinate system, where \(v=\mathbf 1_K\), \(B_a\) is diagonal, and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(h)\).  Define the emission profile of state \(s\) by
\[
 o_s=(B_a(s,s):a\in\mathcal Y).
\]
Every element of the unital algebra generated by the \(B_a\)'s is diagonal and constant on each equivalence class \(s\sim s'\) defined by \(o_s=o_{s'}\).  For the converse inclusion, choose coefficients \((x_a:a\in\mathcal Y)\) outside the finite union of hyperplanes
\[
 \left\{x:\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}x_a\bigl(B_a(s,s)-B_a(s',s')\bigr)=0\right\}
\]
indexed by pairs of distinct profiles.  Then \(X=\sum_a x_aB_a\) has a different diagonal value \(\lambda_c\) on every profile class \(c\).  The Lagrange polynomials
\[
 q_c(X)=\prod_{c'\ne c}\frac{X-\lambda_{c'}I_K}{\lambda_c-\lambda_{c'}}
\]
are the diagonal projectors onto those classes.  Thus
\[
 \mathcal A_O
 =\{\operatorname{diag}(x_1,\ldots,x_K):x_s=x_{s'}\text{ whenever }o_s=o_{s'}\}.       \tag{6}
\]
The hazard-in-emission-algebra assumption says exactly that \(D\) belongs to the right side of (6).  Hence \(D\in\mathcal A_O\) and \(Dv=h\).  Moreover, if \(A\in\mathcal A_O\) and \(Av=0\), then every diagonal entry of \(A\) is zero.  Evaluation at \(v\) is therefore injective on \(\mathcal A_O\), so \(D\) is the unique solution of \(Av=h\) in that algebra.

By the finite-realization theorem, a valid chart is related to the latent realization by a single invertible matrix \(S\).  Thus
\[
 \bar M_a=S^{-1}M_aS,
 \quad \bar K_0=S^{-1}K_0S,
 \quad \bar B_a=S^{-1}B_aS,
 \quad \bar\alpha=\alpha S,
 \quad \bar v=S^{-1}v,
 \quad \bar h=S^{-1}h.                                        \tag{7}
\]
Conjugating (6) shows that the unique canonical solution is
\[
 L=S^{-1}DS,
 \qquad L\bar v=\bar h.                                      \tag{8}
\]
Hazard overlap gives \(1-h_s\ge\varepsilon_h>0\), so \(I_K-D\) and therefore \(I_K-L\) are invertible.  Since \(K_0=(I_K-D)P\), equations (7)--(8) yield
\[
 P_{\mathrm{dk}}=(I_K-L)^{-1}\bar K_0=S^{-1}PS,
 \qquad
 E=S^{-1}\left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}\nu(a)B_a\right)S.     \tag{9}
\]

The timing and future-innovation-independence conditions imply, by conditioning successively on the hidden states, that
\[
 \Pr\!\left(G=g,\,Y_g(\infty)=z_0,\ldots,Y_{g+r}(\infty)=z_r\right)
 =\alpha K_0^gDB_{z_0}PB_{z_1}\cdots PB_{z_r}v,               \tag{10}
\]
where survival for the first \(g\) dates contributes \(K_0^g\), adoption at date \(g\) contributes \(D\), and future counterfactual evolution is not killed.  Summing (10) over all \(z_0,ldots,z_r\), using \(\sum_zB_z=I_K\) and \(Pv=v\), gives
\[
 p_g=\Pr(G=g)=\alpha K_0^gDv=\alpha K_0^gh.                  \tag{11}
\]
The positive-cohort condition permits division by \(p_g\).  Substitution of (7)--(9) into (10), followed by cancellation of adjacent \(S\) and \(S^{-1}\), gives
\[
 \Pr\!\left(Y_g(\infty)=z_0,\ldots,Y_{g+r}(\infty)=z_r\mid G=g\right)
 =\frac{\bar\alpha\bar K_0^gL\bar B_{z_0}P_{\mathrm{dk}}\bar B_{z_1}\cdots P_{\mathrm{dk}}\bar B_{z_r}\bar v}{p_g}. \tag{12}
\]
This is the displayed \(\pi^0_{g,r}\).  It is nonnegative in latent coordinates, and summing its cells gives one by (11), so it is a probability law rather than merely a linear-realization functional.

Multiplying (12) by \(\nu(z_r)\) and summing all cells yields
\[
 \mathbb E\{\nu(Y_{g+r}(\infty))\mid G=g\}
 =\frac{\bar\alpha\bar K_0^gLP_{\mathrm{dk}}^rE\bar v}{p_g}.
                                                                    \tag{13}
\]
The observed treated mean \(\mu^1_{g,r}\) is a conditional mean under \(P_W\), and consistency identifies it with the corresponding mean of the adoption-at-\(g\) potential outcome.  Hence subtracting (13) from \(\mu^1_{g,r}\) proves that the observed-law ATT functional equals the stated causal effect, rather than defining that equality.

Every other valid chart conjugates all factors in (12)--(13) by one common similarity, so the scalar cells are unchanged.  Likewise, in any legal non-permutation realization of the same stopped law, the transported operator in (8) belongs to its current-emission algebra and maps its risk terminal to its adoption terminal.  Injectivity of evaluation forces that operator to equal the realization's actual hazard diagonal.  Thus every legal realization yields (12), proving invariance over the complete legal alias fiber.  On the preregistered chart, the finite-realization formulas compute every factor from words of length at most \(2K-1\), which establishes the last assertion.

Let \(e_k\) denote the \(k\)-th coordinate column, and set
\[
 A=e_i(e_j-e_i)^{\top},\qquad S(t)=I_K+tA.
\]
Then \(A\mathbf 1_K=0\), so \(S(t)\mathbf 1_K=\mathbf 1_K\).  Because states \(i\) and \(j\) have identical emission profiles, \(A B_a=B_a A\) for every \(a\in\mathcal Y\), and hence \(S(t)B_a=B_aS(t)\).  For all sufficiently small \(|t|\), \(S(t)\) is invertible.  Define
\[
 \alpha(t)=\alpha S(t),\quad h(t)=S(t)^{-1}h,
 \quad K_0(t)=S(t)^{-1}K_0S(t),
 \quad P(t)=\{I_K-\operatorname{diag}(h(t))\}^{-1}K_0(t),       \tag{14}
\]
and leave every \(B_a\) unchanged.  At \(t=0\), all entries of \(\alpha\) and \(P\), all hazards, and all emission probabilities are strictly positive.  These inequalities are open.  Hazard overlap also makes the diagonal inverse in (14) continuous near zero.  Therefore, after reducing the neighborhood of zero if necessary, \(\alpha(t)\) is a positive probability row, \(h(t)\) is interior, and \(P(t)\) is entrywise positive.

To check stochasticity rather than assume it, use \(K_0\mathbf 1_K=\mathbf 1_K-h\) and \(S(t)\mathbf 1_K=\mathbf 1_K\):
\[
 K_0(t)\mathbf 1_K
 =S(t)^{-1}K_0\mathbf 1_K
 =\mathbf 1_K-h(t).
\]
Thus \(P(t)\mathbf 1_K=\mathbf 1_K\).  Also \(\alpha(t)\mathbf 1_K=1\).  Hence (14) is a continuum of legal stochastic realizations.  Invertibility of \(K_0(t)\) and predictive rank are preserved by similarity.

Writing \(M_a(t)=B_aK_0(t)\), commutation gives
\[
 M_a(t)=S(t)^{-1}M_aS(t),
 \qquad
 M_w(t)=S(t)^{-1}M_wS(t).                                    \tag{15}
\]
Therefore, for every word \(w\),
\[
 \alpha(t)M_w(t)\mathbf 1_K=\alpha M_w\mathbf 1_K,
 \qquad
 \alpha(t)M_w(t)h(t)=\alpha M_wh.                            \tag{16}
\]
Thus the complete risk- and adoption-terminal stopped law is constant along the path.  The same conditional law of realized post-adoption outcomes can be attached to every member, so the complete observed-panel law is also constant.  Since \(h_i\ne h_j\), the path is nonconstant and, except at isolated parameter values, is not a latent permutation.  Every sufficiently small relative neighborhood in the fixed alias stratum consequently contains a continuum of these legal realizations.

It remains to show that the causal continuation changes.  Express the varying hazard in the original coordinate system as
\[
 J(t)=S(t)\operatorname{diag}(h(t))S(t)^{-1}.
\]
Since \(S'(0)=A\) and \(h'(0)=-Ah\), differentiation gives
\[
 \dot J(0)=[A,D]-\operatorname{diag}(Ah)
 =(h_j-h_i)e_i(e_j-e_i)^{\top},
 \qquad \dot J(0)\mathbf 1_K=0.                              \tag{17}
\]
In these fixed coordinates the de-killed transition associated with \(J\) is \(P_J=(I_K-J)^{-1}K_0\).  Thus
\[
 \dot P_J(0)=(I_K-D)^{-1}\dot J(0)P.                         \tag{18}
\]
The denominator \(p_g=\alpha K_0^gh\) is fixed along the same-observed-law path.  Differentiating the one-step causal numerator and using \(I_K+D(I_K-D)^{-1}=(I_K-D)^{-1}\), equations (17)--(18) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \left.\frac{d}{dt}\mu^0_{g,1}(t)\right|_{t=0}
 &=\frac{\alpha K_0^g\{\dot J(0)Pe+D(I_K-D)^{-1}\dot J(0)Pe\}}{p_g}\\
 &=\frac{(\alpha K_0^g)_i(h_j-h_i)\{(Pe)_j-(Pe)_i\}}{(1-h_i)p_g}. \tag{19}
\end{aligned}
\]
All denominators in (19) are positive: \(1-h_i>0\) by overlap and \(p_g>0\) for a supported cohort.  Moreover, strict positivity of \(\alpha\), \(P\), and \(1-h\) makes every entry of \(\alpha K_0^g\) positive.  The two stated contrasts are nonzero, so (19) is nonzero for every supported \(g\).  Continuity then supplies arbitrarily close path points with different \(\mu^0_{g,1}\).  Keeping the treated-outcome law fixed makes the corresponding ATT values differ with the opposite sign, completing the converse.

Fix a compact subset \(\mathcal K\) of the declared stratum.  On \(\mathcal K\), the fixed lower bounds on \(\sigma_{\min}(H)\), \(\sigma_{\min}(\bar K_0)\), \(\sigma_{\min}(V_F)\), cohort mass, and marginal influence variance keep the corresponding population quantities away from every guarded boundary.  Hazard overlap makes \(I_K-L\) invertible.  Every remaining population inverse and scalar denominator appearing on the inverse-formula branch is continuous and nonzero at each law where that branch represents the displayed functional; compactness then gives a positive lower bound for it on \(\mathcal K\).  Since \(\tau_N=N^{-1/8}\to0\), there is consequently an open neighborhood \(U\) of the population moment set on which, for all sufficiently large \(N\), every gate selects the inverse-formula branch.

The moment envelope implies a uniform second-moment bound.  By independence and Chebyshev's inequality,
\[
 \sup_{P_W\in\mathcal K}P_W\!\left(\|\widehat m-m\|>\epsilon\right)
 \le \frac{C}{N\epsilon^2},                                  \tag{20}
\]
for a constant \(C\) depending only on the fixed dimension \(q\).  Hence \(\widehat m\in U\) with probability tending to one uniformly on \(\mathcal K\), and the fallback branch is asymptotically irrelevant.

On \(U\), every chart coordinate is affine in \(m\), and the inverse-formula branch is a finite composition of matrix addition and multiplication, fixed polynomial evaluation, matrix inversion, and division by cohort masses.  It is therefore twice continuously differentiable.  The load-bearing differentials are
\[
 d(H^{-1})=-H^{-1}(dH)H^{-1},
 \qquad
 d\bar B_a=(d\bar M_a)\bar K_0^{-1}-\bar B_a(d\bar K_0)\bar K_0^{-1}. \tag{21}
\]
Writing \(G_F=V_F^{\top}V_F\) and \(c=G_F^{-1}V_F^{\top}\bar h\), direct differentiation yields
\[
 dc=G_F^{-1}\!\left\{(dV_F)^{\top}\bar h+V_F^{\top}d\bar h
 -\bigl[(dV_F)^{\top}V_F+V_F^{\top}dV_F\bigr]c\right\}.       \tag{22}
\]
The ordinary product rule through every fixed written-order monomial gives \(dL\).  De-killing and propagation then give
\[
 dP_{\mathrm{dk}}=(I_K-L)^{-1}\{d\bar K_0+(dL)P_{\mathrm{dk}}\},
 \qquad
 d(P_{\mathrm{dk}}^r)=\sum_{s=0}^{r-1}P_{\mathrm{dk}}^s(dP_{\mathrm{dk}})P_{\mathrm{dk}}^{r-1-s}. \tag{23}
\]
Finally, the quotient rule differentiates each counterfactual mean, each observed treated mean, and their difference.  Equations (21)--(23) therefore define the advertised joint derivative \(Df(m)\), including the covariance between treated and reconstructed counterfactual components because both are functions of the same panel moment vector.

Compactness and the fixed gaps bound the second derivative of this branch by a common constant.  Taylor's theorem and (20) imply
\[
 \widehat\theta-\theta
 =Df(m)(\widehat m-m)+R_N,
 \qquad
 \|R_N\|\le C\|\widehat m-m\|^2=O_{P_W}(N^{-1}),             \tag{24}
\]
uniformly on \(\mathcal K\).  Identification gives \(f(m)=\theta\); it is not imposed as a definition of the causal target.  Since
\[
 Df(m)(\widehat m-m)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^NDf(m)\{Z(W_i)-m\}
 =\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\varphi(W_i),                            \tag{25}
\]
multiplication of (24) by \(\sqrt N\) proves the displayed influence expansion.

For any sequence \(P_{W,N}\in\mathcal K\), the uniform \((2+\delta)\)-moment bound implies the Lindeberg condition for \(N^{-1/2}\varphi(W_i)\).  Every subsequence of the bounded covariance matrices has a further convergent subsequence, and the cited multivariate Lindeberg--Feller theorem applies there.  This subsequence argument gives the required uniform fixed-dimensional Gaussian approximation.  Continuity of \(Df\), consistency of \(\widehat m\), and uniform integrability from the same moment bound give
\[
 \widehat\Sigma
 =\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\varphi_i\widehat\varphi_i^{\top}+o_{P_W}(1)
 \longrightarrow_{P_W}\mathbb E_{P_W}[\varphi(W)\varphi(W)^{\top}]=\Sigma, \tag{26}
\]
uniformly on \(\mathcal K\), where \(\widehat\varphi_i=Df(\widehat m)\{Z(W_i)-\widehat m\}\) on the pass branch.

If \(\xi_1,ldots,\xi_N\) are independent standard Gaussian multipliers, then conditionally on the panels,
\[
 \frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_{i=1}^N\xi_i\widehat\varphi_i
 \sim N(0,\widehat\Sigma).                                   \tag{27}
\]
Equation (26) therefore makes the conditional law in (27) converge to the same Gaussian law as (25).  The bound \(\min_j\Sigma_{jj}\ge\kappa_V\) validates studentization.  Because \(|\mathcal G|\) is fixed, the maximum of the absolute studentized coordinates has a continuous distribution; continuity follows since each boundary event is contained in a finite union of zero-probability Gaussian hyperplanes.  Its conditional multiplier quantile consequently yields simultaneous limiting noncoverage \(\alpha_0\).  Equations (20) and (24) show that replacing all outputs by their fixed fallback values off the pass branch changes none of these conclusions.

Write \(\eta=\eta_N\), \(\zeta=\zeta_N\), and \(S=S_{\star}\).  The first realization converges as \((\eta,\zeta)\to(0,0)\) to a model whose initial probabilities, transitions, emissions, hazards, and survival probabilities are all strictly positive.  For the second realization,
\[
 \alpha^{(1)}=\left(\frac{31}{100},\frac{39}{100},\frac3{10}\right),
 \qquad
 h^{(1)}=\left(\frac3{20}-\frac54\eta,\frac3{20}+\frac54\eta,\frac9{20}\right)^{\top}, \tag{28}
\]
and at \(\eta=0\),
\[
 P^{(1)}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 49/80&5/16&3/40\\
 3/16&39/80&13/40\\
 11/100&19/100&7/10
 \end{pmatrix}.                                                \tag{29}
\]
Every displayed entry in (28)--(29) is positive.  The formula defining \(P_N^{(1)}\) is continuous wherever the components of \(1-h_N^{(1)}\) are positive.  Hence all its entries, all hazards and survivals, and both binary emission probabilities are strictly positive for sufficiently large \(N\).  Directly,
\[
 p_0=\alpha_{\star}h_N^{(0)}=\frac{5\eta+12}{50}>0.            \tag{30}
\]
Stochasticity of \(P_N^{(1)}\) follows without an extra assumption: since \(S\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_3\),
\[
 K_{0,N}^{(1)}\mathbf 1_3
 =S^{-1}(\mathbf 1_3-h_N^{(0)})
 =\mathbf 1_3-h_N^{(1)},
\]
so \(P_N^{(1)}\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_3\).

When \(\zeta=0\), the first two emission probabilities coincide and therefore \(SB_a^{\star}=B_a^{\star}S\) for \(a=0,1\).  It follows exactly that
\[
 M_{a,N}^{(1)}=S^{-1}M_{a,N}^{(0)}S,
 \quad \alpha_N^{(1)}=\alpha_{\star}S,
 \quad h_N^{(1)}=S^{-1}h_N^{(0)},
 \quad S\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_3.                              \tag{31}
\]
For every stopped word \(w\), multiplying (31) gives equality of both terminal series:
\[
 \alpha_N^{(1)}M_{w,N}^{(1)}\mathbf 1_3
 =\alpha_{\star}M_{w,N}^{(0)}\mathbf 1_3,
 \qquad
 \alpha_N^{(1)}M_{w,N}^{(1)}h_N^{(1)}
 =\alpha_{\star}M_{w,N}^{(0)}h_N^{(0)}.                       \tag{32}
\]
The treated-outcome law is common by construction, so the complete observed laws agree at \(\zeta=0\).

The support of a six-date stopped panel is finite.  On its common nonzero support, strict positivity at the limit supplies a cell-probability lower bound independent of sufficiently small \(\eta,\zeta\).  Every cell probability is a finite product and sum of entries of the displayed matrices and is therefore analytic near the limit.  Equation (32) says that the difference of corresponding cells vanishes at \(\zeta=0\), uniformly for small \(\eta\); hence
\[
 \max_x|p_{\eta,\zeta}(x)-q_{\eta,\zeta}(x)|=O(\zeta).       \tag{33}
\]
Using \(\log u\le u-1\),
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(p_{\eta,\zeta},q_{\eta,\zeta})
 \le\sum_x\frac{\{p_{\eta,\zeta}(x)-q_{\eta,\zeta}(x)\}^2}{q_{\eta,\zeta}(x)}
 =O(\zeta^2).                                                  \tag{34}
\]
Expansion of the product log likelihood gives additivity of relative entropy, so at \(\zeta_N=N^{-1}\),
\[
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left((P_{W,N}^{(0)})^{\otimes N},(P_{W,N}^{(1)})^{\otimes N}\right)
 =N\operatorname{KL}(P_{W,N}^{(0)},P_{W,N}^{(1)})=O(N^{-1}).   \tag{35}
\]
Alternatively, the chi-square quantity on the right of (34) is \(O(\zeta^2)\), and
\[
 1+\chi^2(p^{\otimes N},q^{\otimes N})=\{1+\chi^2(p,q)\}^{N}.
\]
Thus the product chi-square divergence is \(O(N^{-1})\).  Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
 \|p^{\otimes N}-q^{\otimes N}\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
 \le\frac12\sqrt{\chi^2(p^{\otimes N},q^{\otimes N})}=O(N^{-1/2})\to0. \tag{36}
\]

We next reproduce the declared singular-value constant.  At \(\eta=\zeta=0\), direct rational multiplication for the corrected chart gives
\[
 H=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&6/25&2847/25000\\
 509/1000&2847/25000&1506459/25000000\\
 251/1000&3651/50000&601221/25000000
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det H=\frac{257499}{31250000000}\ne0.                       \tag{37}
\]
For this chart let
\[
 C(\eta,\zeta)=\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf 1_3&h_N^{(0)}&B_{0,N}^{\star}K_{0,N}^{(0)}h_N^{(0)}\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The realization factorization proved for the finite chart implies
\[
 V_D(\eta,\zeta)
 =C(\eta,\zeta)^{-1}
 \begin{bmatrix}\mathbf 1_3&B_{1,N}^{\star}\mathbf 1_3&(B_{1,N}^{\star})^2\mathbf 1_3\end{bmatrix}. \tag{38}
\]
At \(\eta=0\), exact simplification of (38) yields
\[
 V_D(0,0)=
 \begin{pmatrix}1&-1/10&-13/50\\0&2&2\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det V_D(0,\zeta)=-\frac{500\zeta(5\zeta-3)}{51(5\zeta-1)}. \tag{39}
\]
The product of the two nonzero singular values of \(V_D(0,0)\) is the square root of the sum of squares of its two-by-two minors, namely
\[
 \sigma_1\{V_D(0,0)\}\sigma_2\{V_D(0,0)\}=\frac{2\sqrt{1266}}{25}. \tag{40}
\]
Since the product of all three singular values is the absolute determinant, (39)--(40), continuity, and \(\eta_N\to0\) imply
\[
 \sigma_3\{V_D(\eta_N,\zeta_N)\}
 =\left(\frac{6250}{17\sqrt{1266}}+o(1)\right)\zeta_N
 =\{10.332710061\ldots+o(1)\}\zeta_N.                         \tag{41}
\]
Indeed, at \(\zeta=0\) the first two latent entries of each of \(\mathbf 1_3\), \(B_{1,N}^{\star}\mathbf 1_3\), and \((B_{1,N}^{\star})^2\mathbf 1_3\) agree, so (38) has rank exactly two for every sufficiently small \(\eta\).  Thus there is no term depending only on \(\eta\); the first-order coefficient in \(\zeta\) is continuous at \(\eta=0\), which justifies evaluating it through (39)--(40) along \(\eta_N\to0\).
In particular this singular value is positive for large \(N\), and
\[
 \frac{\sigma_3(V_D)}{\rho_N}
 =O\!\left(\frac{N^{-1}}{\sqrt{\log N/N}}\right)\to0.         \tag{42}
\]
Thus the displayed population moment lies in the sampling-noise component \(0<\sigma_3(V_D)\le\rho_N\) of the gray zone.

Finally, direct substitution in the two latent causal means gives the exact difference
\[
 \Delta(\eta,\zeta)
 :=(\mu^0_{0,1})^{(1)}-(\mu^0_{0,1})^{(0)}
 =-\frac{3\{87500\eta^3\zeta+18000\eta^2\zeta+9000\eta^2+22015\eta\zeta+53550\eta-3468\zeta\}}
 {400(5\eta+12)(25\eta-17)(25\eta+17)}.                      \tag{43}
\]
All denominators in (43) are nonzero for sufficiently small positive \(\eta\).  Since \(\zeta_N=\eta_N^4\), expansion at zero yields
\[
 \Delta(\eta_N,\zeta_N)=\frac{63}{544}\eta_N+o(\eta_N).      \tag{44}
\]
The treated outcome is the same deterministic constant in both laws, so the ATT difference is \(-\Delta\).

To prove the final impossibility statement, let \(C_N\) be any confidence band with asymptotic coverage at least \(1-\alpha_0\) under both product laws, and write their two ATT values as \(\theta_{0,N}\) and \(\theta_{1,N}\).  By (36), under the first product law,
\[
 \Pr(\theta_{0,N}\in C_N)\ge1-\alpha_0-o(1),
 \qquad
 \Pr(\theta_{1,N}\in C_N)\ge1-\alpha_0-o(1).
\]
The union bound therefore gives
\[
 \Pr\bigl(\theta_{0,N},\theta_{1,N}\in C_N\bigr)
 \ge1-2\alpha_0-o(1)>0.                                      \tag{45}
\]
On the event in (45), \(\operatorname{diam}(C_N)\ge|\theta_{1,N}-\theta_{0,N}|=(63/544+o(1))N^{-1/4}\), contradicting diameter \(o(N^{-1/4})\) in probability.  This completes every assertion of the proposition.

added_lemmas.statement: Let \(X_{n1},\ldots,X_{nk_n}\) be independent, mean-zero random vectors of a fixed finite dimension.  If the sum of their covariance matrices converges to \(\Sigma\) and the multivariate Lindeberg condition holds, then \(\sum_iX_{ni}\) converges in distribution to the centered Gaussian law with covariance \(\Sigma\).

proofs.proof_tex:
Work throughout at the fixed values \(K=3\), \(T=5\), \(g=0\), and \(r=1\) in \(\mathfrak W_{2/185}\).  Put
\[
 v=(1,1,1)^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 e=(1/5,1/5,4/5)^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 B_1=\operatorname{diag}(e),\qquad B_0=I_3-B_1.
\]
Thus both emission probabilities are strictly positive in every state.  From the displayed \(P\) and \(h\) in Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}exact\text{-}negative\text{-}fiber}\), direct multiplication gives
\[
 K_0=(I_3-\operatorname{diag}(h))P
 =\begin{pmatrix}
 27/50&27/100&9/100\\
 7/50&7/20&21/100\\
 11/200&11/100&77/200
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The inverse of the specified mixing matrix and the transformed initial distribution and hazard are
\[
 S_{\star}^{-1}
 =\begin{pmatrix}9/8&-1/8&0\\-1/8&9/8&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \alpha'=\alpha S_{\star}=(31/100,39/100,3/10),
 \qquad
 h'=S_{\star}^{-1}h=(3/40,13/40,9/20)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 K_0'=S_{\star}^{-1}K_0S_{\star}
 =\begin{pmatrix}
 557/1000&293/1000&3/40\\
 117/1000&333/1000&9/40\\
 121/2000&209/2000&77/200
 \end{pmatrix},
\]
and de-killing according to the construction yields
\[
 P'=(I_3-\operatorname{diag}(h'))^{-1}K_0'
 =\begin{pmatrix}
 557/925&293/925&3/37\\
 13/75&37/75&1/3\\
 11/100&19/100&7/10
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
Every displayed entry of \(\alpha,\alpha',P,P'\), both emission probability vectors, and \(h,h'\) is positive.  The entries of each initial row sum to one.  The rows of \(P'\) sum respectively to
\[
 \frac{557+293+75}{925}=1,\qquad
 \frac{13+37+25}{75}=1,\qquad
 \frac{11+19+70}{100}=1,
\]
and the row-stochasticity of \(P\) follows in the same way from its displayed entries.  Moreover every coordinate of both hazards belongs to \([1/20,19/20]\).  This proves strict positivity, stochasticity, and hazard overlap for both realizations.  The killed dynamics are invertible because
\[
 \det(K_0)=\frac{4851}{100000}>0,
 \qquad
 \det(K_0')=\det(S_{\star}^{-1}K_0S_{\star})
 =\det(K_0)>0.
\]

We next prove equality of the observed stopped laws rather than presupposing it.  Since the first two states have the same emission distribution, \(B_aS_{\star}=S_{\star}B_a\) for each \(a\in\{0,1\}\); also \(S_{\star}v=v\).  Hence, for the killed observable operators of Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}stopped\text{-}series}\),
\[
 M_a'=B_aK_0'
 =B_aS_{\star}^{-1}K_0S_{\star}
 =S_{\star}^{-1}M_aS_{\star}.
\]
For every word \(w=(a_1,\ldots,a_\ell)\), including the empty word with \(M_\epsilon=I_3\), telescoping therefore gives
\[
 M_w'=S_{\star}^{-1}M_wS_{\star}.
\]
Using \(\alpha'=\alpha S_{\star}\), \(h'=S_{\star}^{-1}h\), and \(S_{\star}v=v\), the two terminal series agree term by term:
\[
 F_R'(w)=\alpha'M_w'v
 =\alpha M_wv=F_R(w),
 \qquad
 F_A'(w)=\alpha'M_w'h'
 =\alpha M_wh=F_A(w).
\]
This equality holds for all word lengths and hence, in particular, for every stopped-word observable available on dates \(0,\ldots,5\).  Each atom of a stopped panel is specified by its pre-adoption word together with an adoption or risk terminal; after adoption, all outcome coordinates are the same fixed constant in the two constructions.  Thus the preceding equalities imply equality of the complete observed laws \(P_W'=P_W\), not merely equality of selected moments.

For completeness, consider the prefix tuple \((\epsilon,0,1)\) and terminal-suffix tuple \(((\epsilon,R),(\epsilon,A),(0,R))\).  Substitution into Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}stopped\text{-}series}\) gives the stopped-Hankel minor
\[
 H_\star=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 1&57/200&473/1000\\
 473/1000&24629/200000&242957/1000000\\
 121/500&7843/100000&46519/500000
 \end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det(H_\star)=\frac{42471}{625000000}\ne0.
\]
A three-state linear realization has predictive Hankel rank at most three, because every Hankel entry factors through a row and a column in \(\mathbb R^3\).  The nonzero \(3\)-by-\(3\) minor gives rank at least three.  Hence the predictive rank is exactly \(K=3\).  Since all stopped series coordinates coincide, this same minor certifies full predictive rank for the primed realization.

It remains to calculate the causal counterfactuals and to keep them distinct from the common observed law.  The time-zero adoption mass is the empty-word adoption terminal, so
\[
 p_0=F_A(\epsilon)=\alpha h=\frac{57}{200},
 \qquad
 p_0'=\alpha'h'=\alpha S_{\star}S_{\star}^{-1}h
 =\frac{57}{200}>0.
\]
In either constructed realization, conditional on \(S_0=s\), adoption at zero has probability \(h_s\), and the never-adopt untreated chain subsequently uses transition matrix \(P\); the primed realization has the analogous property with \(h'\) and \(P'\).  Thus Bayes' rule and iterated expectation give, for \(j=0,1\),
\[
 \Pr(S_0=s\mid G=0)=\frac{\alpha_sh_s}{p_0},
 \qquad
 \mu^0_{0,j}=\frac{\alpha\operatorname{diag}(h)P^je}{p_0},
\]
and
\[
 \Pr'(S_0=s\mid G=0)=\frac{\alpha_s'h_s'}{p_0'},
 \qquad
 (\mu^0_{0,j})'=\frac{\alpha'\operatorname{diag}(h')(P')^je}{p_0'}.
\]
These are also exactly the latent-coordinate evaluations of Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}counterfactual\text{-}functional}\), where \(L=\operatorname{diag}(h)\), \(P_{\mathrm{dk}}=P\), and \(E v=e\), and similarly for the primed realization.  The division is valid by the displayed strict positivity of \(p_0\).

The required products are
\[
 \alpha\operatorname{diag}(h)
 =(3/100,3/25,27/200),
 \qquad
 \alpha'\operatorname{diag}(h')
 =(93/4000,507/4000,27/200),
\]
\[
 Pe=(13/50,19/50,31/50)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 P'e=(46/185,2/5,31/50)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
It follows first that
\[
 \alpha\operatorname{diag}(h)e
 =\alpha'\operatorname{diag}(h')e
 =\frac{69}{500},
 \qquad
 \mu^0_{0,0}=(\mu^0_{0,0})'
 =\frac{69/500}{57/200}=\frac{46}{95}.
\]
For the next-period untreated outcome,
\[
 \alpha\operatorname{diag}(h)Pe=\frac{1371}{10000},
 \qquad
 \alpha'\operatorname{diag}(h')P'e=\frac{51867}{370000},
\]
and therefore
\[
 \mu^0_{0,1}=\frac{1371/10000}{57/200}=\frac{457}{950},
 \qquad
 (\mu^0_{0,1})'=\frac{51867/370000}{57/200}
 =\frac{17289}{35150}.
\]
Their exact separation is
\[
 (\mu^0_{0,1})'-\mu^0_{0,1}
 =\frac{17289}{35150}-\frac{457}{950}
 =\frac{2}{185}>0.
\]
Finally, if the common post-adoption outcome constant is \(c\), then the common observed treated mean is \(\mu^1_{0,1}=c\).  Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}att\text{-}functional}\) consequently yields
\[
 (\tau_{0,1})'-\tau_{0,1}
 =\{c-(\mu^0_{0,1})'\}-\{c-\mu^0_{0,1}\}
 =-\frac{2}{185}.
\]
Here \(g+r=1\le T=5\), so no boundary convention is invoked, and every denominator used above is positive.  No limiting argument is used.  Thus an identical observed-panel law has two distinct causal ATT values, with the asserted exact gap.

Fix a law on a valid predeclared stopped-Hankel chart, so that \(H_{\mathcal U,\mathcal V}\) is nonsingular, and fix \((g,r)\) with \(0\leq g\leq g+r\leq T\) and \(p_g>0\).  The horizon and predictive-rank assumptions, together with the finite-realization theorem, imply that the latent stopped realization and the canonical realization are related by an invertible matrix \(S\).  Choose the orientation of \(S\) so that
\[
 \bar\alpha=\alpha S,\qquad
 \bar M_a=S^{-1}B_aK_0S,\qquad
 \bar v=S^{-1}v,qquad
 \bar h=S^{-1}h.
\]
The emission probabilities sum to one in each hidden state under the homogeneous untreated HMM assumption, hence \(\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}B_a=I_K\).  Therefore, using the definitions of \(\bar K_0\) and \(\bar B_a\), and using nonsingularity of \(K_0\),
\[
 \bar K_0=\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}\bar M_a
 =S^{-1}K_0S,
 \qquad
 \bar B_a=\bar M_a\bar K_0^{-1}=S^{-1}B_aS.                                      \tag{1}
\]
In particular, the canonical emission algebra is the similarity transform of the algebra generated by the diagonal matrices \(B_a\).

Suppose first that \(K=1\).  Row stochasticity of the one-by-one transition matrix gives \(P=1\), while \(B_a=b_a\), \(\sum_a b_a=1\), \(D=h\), and \(Q=1-h\).  Thus
\[
 K_0=QP=1-h.
\]
The current-state hazard assumption gives, for every supported cohort \(g\),
\[
 p_g=\Pr(G=g)=\alpha K_0^g h=(1-h)^g h,                                      \tag{2}
\]
because \(\alpha=v=1\).  Hazard overlap gives \(0<h<1\), so every division and the inverse below are valid.  In one dimension the emission algebra is the scalar algebra.  Since \(\bar h=h\bar v\) and \(\bar v\neq0\) (indeed \(\bar\alpha\bar v=F_R(\epsilon)=1\)), the defining equation \(L\bar v=\bar h\) has the unique scalar solution \(L=h\).  Consequently
\[
 P_{\mathrm{dk}}=(1-L)^{-1}\bar K_0=(1-h)^{-1}(1-h)=1.                         \tag{3}
\]
Substitution of (2)--(3) and \(\bar B_a=b_a\) into the counterfactual functional yields
\[
 \pi^0_{g,r}(z_0,\ldots,z_r)
 =\frac{\bar\alpha(1-h)^gh\bigl(\prod_{j=0}^r b_{z_j}\bigr)\bar v}
 {(1-h)^gh}
 =\prod_{j=0}^r b_{z_j}.                                                        \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, \(E=\sum_a\nu(a)b_a\), and the same substitution gives
\[
 \mu^0_{g,r}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}\nu(a)b_a.                                  \tag{5}
\]
Thus the first reduction follows, including the asserted support and positivity conditions.

Now suppose that the emission-profile vectors are pairwise distinct.  Write
\[
 x_s=(B_a(s,s):a\in\mathcal Y)\in\mathbb R^{|\mathcal Y|}.
\]
For each ordered pair \(s\neq t\), choose \(a(s,t)\in\mathcal Y\) such that \(B_{a(s,t)}(s,s)\neq B_{a(s,t)}(t,t)\); such a coordinate exists by pairwise distinctness.  Define the explicit interpolation polynomial
\[
 q_s(x)=\prod_{t\neq s}
 \frac{x_{a(s,t)}-B_{a(s,t)}(t,t)}
 {B_{a(s,t)}(s,s)-B_{a(s,t)}(t,t)}.                                             \tag{6}
\]
Every denominator in (6) is nonzero by its construction.  The factor indexed by \(t\) vanishes at \(x_t\), whereas every factor equals one at \(x_s\); hence \(q_s(x_u)=\mathbf 1\{u=s\}\).  Since the \(B_a\)'s are commuting diagonal matrices, polynomial evaluation in (6) gives
\[
 q_s((B_a)_{a\in\mathcal Y})=\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf 1\{u=s\}:1\leq u\leq K).
\]
These \(K\) coordinate projectors span every diagonal matrix, so the latent-coordinate emission algebra contains \(D\).

By (1), \(\widetilde L=S^{-1}DS\) belongs to \(\mathcal A_O\), and
\[
 \widetilde L\bar v=S^{-1}DS S^{-1}v=S^{-1}Dv=S^{-1}h=\bar h.                  \tag{7}
\]
The evaluation map on \(\mathcal A_O\) is injective: every \(A\in\mathcal A_O\) has the form \(A=S^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(d)S\), and
\[
 A\bar v=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 S^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(d)v=S^{-1}d=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A=0.                                               \tag{8}
\]
Equations (7)--(8) and the definition of the hazard lift therefore give
\[
 L=S^{-1}DS.                                                                     \tag{9}
\]
Because hazard overlap implies that \(Q=I_K-D\) is invertible, (1), (9), and \(K_0=QP\) imply
\[
 P_{\mathrm{dk}}
 =(I_K-L)^{-1}\bar K_0
 =S^{-1}Q^{-1}K_0S
 =S^{-1}PS.                                                                       \tag{10}
\]
Also, with \(E_0=\sum_a\nu(a)B_a\),
\[
 E=S^{-1}E_0S,
 \qquad E_0v=e.                                                                  \tag{11}
\]
Substituting (1) and (9)--(11) into the displayed counterfactual functional and cancelling adjacent factors \(SS^{-1}\) gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \pi^0_{g,r}(z_0,\ldots,z_r)
 &=\frac{\alpha K_0^gDB_{z_0}PB_{z_1}\cdots PB_{z_r}v}{p_g},\\
 \mu^0_{g,r}
 &=\frac{\alpha K_0^gDP^re}{p_g}.
 \end{aligned}                                                                  \tag{12}
\]
The current-state hazard and future-innovation-independence assumptions also verify the causal content of (12), rather than merely its algebraic form.  Conditional on the state at date \(g\), adoption is independent of the current untreated emission and all later untreated innovations, so
\[
 \Pr\{G=g,Y_g(\infty)=z_0,\ldots,Y_{g+r}(\infty)=z_r\}
 =\alpha K_0^gDB_{z_0}PB_{z_1}\cdots PB_{z_r}v.                                 \tag{13}
\]
Division of (13) by the positive cohort mass \(p_g\) proves that the first line of (12) is the conditional untreated path law.  Summing its last coordinate after weighting by \(\nu\), and summing all preceding coordinates, proves the second line of (12).  Thus the observed-law functional equals the stated counterfactual quantity under the declared causal assumptions; it is not being made causal by definition.

Next suppose \(h_s=\lambda\) for every state.  Since \(h\in(0,1)^K\), \(0<\lambda<1\), and
\[
 D=\lambda I_K,\qquad Q=(1-\lambda)I_K,qquad \bar h=S^{-1}h=\lambda\bar v.
\]
The matrix \(\lambda I_K\) lies in the unital algebra \(\mathcal A_O\) and solves \(L\bar v=\bar h\).  Injectivity follows by the same argument as (8), without pairwise distinctness: every polynomial in the simultaneously diagonal matrices \(B_a\) is diagonal, so its similarity transform annihilates \(\bar v=S^{-1}v\) only if that diagonal is zero.  Hence the hazard-lift definition gives \(L=\lambda I_K\).  Using (1) and \(K_0=(1-\lambda)P\),
\[
 P_{\mathrm{dk}}
 =(1-\lambda)^{-1}\bar K_0
 =S^{-1}PS,                                                                       \tag{14}
\]
which proves the constant-hazard reduction.

Finally take \(r=0\), and do not impose the hazard-in-emission-algebra restriction.  On any valid canonical chart of the ambient stopped model, current-state hazard and conditional independence of adoption from \(Y_g(\infty)\) give, for every \(a\in\mathcal Y\),
\[
 \Pr\{G=g,Y_g(\infty)=a\}=\alpha K_0^gB_ah.
\]
Consequently, using (1), the terminal similarity relations, and \(p_g>0\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mu^0_{g,0}
 &=\frac{\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}\nu(a)\alpha K_0^gB_ah}{p_g}\\
 &=\frac{\bar\alpha\bar K_0^g
 \left(\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}\nu(a)\bar B_a\right)\bar h}{p_g}
 =\frac{\bar\alpha\bar K_0^gE\bar h}{p_g}.
 \end{aligned}                                                                  \tag{15}
\]
This last derivation uses the directly observed adoption-terminal stopped probabilities and never constructs \(L\); therefore it remains valid without the hazard-algebra restriction.  Equations (4), (5), (12), (14), and (15) establish all four reductions.

proposed.statement: If \(K=1\), write \(b_a=\Pr(Y_t(\infty)=a)\) and let \(h\) be the scalar hazard. Then \(P=1\), \(K_0=1-h\), \(p_g=(1-h)^gh\), \(L=h\), \(P_{\mathrm{dk}}=1\), \(\pi^0_{g,r}(z_0,\ldots,z_r)=\prod_{j=0}^r b_{z_j}\), and \(\mu^0_{g,r}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal Y}\nu(a)b_a\). If the \(K\) emission-profile vectors \(\{(B_a(s,s):a\in\mathcal Y):1\le s\le K\}\) are pairwise distinct, multivariate polynomial interpolation gives every diagonal matrix in the latent-coordinate emission algebra; hence the canonical \(L\) is similar to \(D\), \(P_{\mathrm{dk}}\) is similar to \(P\), and the observable formulas reduce exactly to \(\pi^0_{g,r}(z_0,\ldots,z_r)=\alpha K_0^gDB_{z_0}PB_{z_1}\cdots PB_{z_r}v/p_g\) and \(\mu^0_{g,r}=\alpha K_0^gDP^re/p_g\). If \(h_s=\lambda\) for every state, then \(L=\lambda I_K\) and \(P_{\mathrm{dk}}\) is similar to \(P\). For \(r=0\), \(\mu^0_{g,0}=\bar\alpha\bar K_0^gE\bar h/p_g\) without the hazard-algebra restriction.
proposed.justification: These reductions prevent the new formula from contradicting ordinary identified HMMs or the mechanically identified contemporaneous cohort mean.
proposed.gap: The reductions are sanity checks rather than novelty claims.
proposed.consumer: They give implementers diagnostic benchmarks for one-state, distinct-emission, constant-hazard, and contemporaneous-effect cases.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The proof uses the frozen minimal-realization similarity, the stopped-HMM timing assumptions, chart rank and invertibility, hazard overlap, and positive cohort support; these load-bearing dependencies were absent from the original metadata.
